items.headline: Oracle adds Google, Cerebras and SambaNova chips to its AI cloud while expanding its Nvidia order
items.body: At its investor day on October 27, Oracle said it will run Google's TPU accelerators in its own data centres, the first time Google's AI chips will sit in a rival cloud provider's facilities, and will add inference chips from Cerebras and SambaNova. Oracle simultaneously enlarged its Nvidia commitment, scaling Vera Rubin systems to what it called multi-gigawatt levels, while swapping some Nvidia networking hardware for its own Acceleron silicon. It held its fiscal 2027 capital-expenditure target at roughly $90 billion to $95 billion.
items.plain: Oracle rents out computing power by the hour. Almost all AI computing runs on chips from one company, Nvidia, which gives Nvidia enormous pricing power. Oracle is now installing chips from three competitors alongside Nvidia's. The split matters: building a model still needs Nvidia, but running a finished one to answer questions, called inference, is the cheaper and far larger ongoing job, and rival chips are good enough at it.
items.why: Inference is where Nvidia's lock on the market is thinnest, and its largest customers are now wiring alternatives into their buildings rather than merely threatening to.

items.headline: Netanyahu's bloc leads Israel's count with 54 seats, short of a majority
items.body: With about 84 percent of Tuesday's ballots counted on Wednesday, the Likud-led bloc held 54 of the Knesset's 120 seats and the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot held 49, with Arab parties on 17. Sixty-one seats are needed to govern. Likud remained the largest single party at 27 to 28 seats and Eisenkot's Yashar party stood at about 21. Eisenkot has ruled out serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotating premiership. The count is not final and seat totals moved overnight.
items.plain: Israelis do not vote for a prime minister directly. They vote for parties, which win seats in a 120-member parliament, and whoever assembles 61 of those seats forms a government. Netanyahu's side has 54, so it needs partners. His opponents have 49, so they need partners too. The only group large enough to push either side past 61 is the Arab parties, with 17 seats, and Israeli governments have almost never included them.
items.why: Netanyahu does not need to win the count, only to outlast it: every week without a 61-seat alternative leaves him in office as caretaker prime minister.

items.headline: US consumer confidence rises for the first time since June
items.body: The Conference Board's consumer confidence index rose to 91.7 in October from a revised 84.2 in September, the first increase in four months, against forecasts of about 81.0. The present situation component rose 8.6 points to 120.4. The expectations component rose 6.9 points to 72.6, still below the 80 level the Board associates with recession risk. The Board credited petrol prices falling from an average $4.48 to $4.27 a gallon, and noted that spending intentions for services and durable goods weakened.
items.plain: This survey asks thousands of Americans how the economy feels now and how they expect it to look in six months. Both rose, by much more than forecasters guessed, but the two halves disagree. Views of today jumped, tracking cheaper petrol, which people notice weekly. Views of the future improved less and stayed in the range the Board treats as a warning sign. Respondents also said they plan to spend less on services and big-ticket goods.
items.why: Confidence that improves because fuel got cheaper while purchase plans weaken is a sentiment rebound rather than a demand rebound, and the Fed, which decides rates this afternoon, cares about the second.

items.headline: FDA and CMS move to widen gene-therapy access beyond sickle-cell disease
items.body: The Department of Health and Human Services said on October 27 that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will expand its Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model past sickle-cell disease to other rare diseases and some cancers. Under the model CMS negotiates outcomes-based agreements with manufacturers on behalf of state Medicaid programmes, tying payment partly to whether the treatment works; 33 states plus the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have signed on. The FDA issued draft guidance the same day on personalised gene therapies for rare genetic diseases.
items.plain: A gene therapy fixes a faulty gene once and can cost two to three million dollars in a single bill. Medicaid, the government insurance programme for people with low incomes, covers many patients with inherited diseases, and no state budget absorbs bills like that easily. So CMS negotiates one price for all the states at once and ties part of the payment to whether the patient improves. Without a buyer, nobody develops a cure for a few hundred patients.
items.why: The binding constraint on gene therapy has shifted from whether the science works to whether anyone can pay for it, so the payment mechanism now decides which diseases get cures.

items.headline: China's AI and chip stocks have given up about $480 billion since July
items.body: A Reuters analysis published October 26 found the STAR 50 index, which tracks mainland China's leading AI and semiconductor companies, has fallen roughly 40 percent in under four months from its July peak, erasing about $480 billion in market value. GPU designers MetaX and Moore Threads, up 700 and 400 percent on their debuts last year, have each halved since July. Optical-component makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink are down about 60 percent, partly on Washington's moves toward barring them from US data centres. The index still trades near 100 times past earnings, against roughly 30 for the Nasdaq 100.
items.plain: Chinese investors bid AI and chip companies up to extraordinary prices this year, then sold. Traders name no single trigger, pointing to valuations, tax bills and the risk that the United States bars Chinese networking gear from American data centres, removing a large customer. Note the figure that does not fit the word crash: even after losing 40 percent, these shares cost about 100 times yearly earnings, where US tech trades near 30.
items.why: China's AI share prices deflated without a matching cut to AI spending, which is the cleanest live test of whether a market's AI valuations and its AI build-out are the same thing.

items.headline: Finland and Norway's leaders hold a call with Putin, the first such contact in over a year
items.body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke with Vladimir Putin for about 90 minutes on October 27, the first call between pro-Ukraine European leaders and the Kremlin in more than a year. Stubb said it followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo and was prepared in coordination with Ukraine and the United States. Store said there are big differences in views. The Kremlin said Putin criticised EU and NATO policy as prolonging the war but agreed to keep direct telephone contact. Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators have agreed to technical talks in early November, reportedly in Abu Dhabi.
items.plain: Since the invasion most European leaders have refused to telephone Putin at all, on the reasoning that a call is itself a reward that treats him as a normal head of state. Finland and Norway both border Russia, so they have the most to lose from a frozen conflict next door. They cleared the call with Kyiv and Washington first, which is what makes it diplomacy rather than defection. Nothing was agreed; the point was to open a line before next month's talks.
items.why: Two NATO governments on Russia's border have decided the cost of refusing to talk now exceeds the cost of legitimising Putin, which is a shift in European posture rather than a single phone call.

sources.outlet: Office of the President of Finland

items.headline: CoreWeave's default insurance hits a record, pricing better-than-even odds of failure
items.body: Credit default swaps on CoreWeave, the AI cloud provider that rents Nvidia capacity to customers including OpenAI and Microsoft, reached a record. Bloomberg, citing ICE Data Services, put the five-year contract at an intraday peak of 1,194.5 basis points, implying a more than 60 percent chance of default within five years; CNBC reported levels nearer 1,038 to 1,145, and an October 27 reading put it at 1,148 against 835 a month earlier. The shares are down about 36 percent this month. Second-quarter accounts showed $35.6 billion of debt plus $16.3 billion of lease liabilities, about $20.7 billion of it due through 2030. CoreWeave reports a roughly $104 billion backlog and has announced no default.
items.plain: A credit default swap is insurance against a company failing to pay its debts, so its price is a market estimate of that risk. CoreWeave's has never been this expensive. The cause is not weak demand, the usual reason companies fail: it holds orders worth about $104 billion. It borrowed heavily to buy chips and must refinance while interest rates rise. Its stock and bond investors disagree sharply, and both cannot be right.
items.why: The AI build-out's fragile point is the financing schedule rather than customer demand, and CoreWeave is the first large test of what happens when those two diverge.

items.headline: A judge lets Eli Lilly keep running ads comparing its weight-loss drug with Novo Nordisk's
items.body: US District Judge Zahid Quraishi in Trenton denied Novo Nordisk's request for a preliminary injunction against Eli Lilly advertisements comparing the two companies' drugs directly, writing that Novo's showing of irreparable harm was inadequate to warrant the extraordinary relief it seeks. He found the advertisements had negligible market impact between April and July, and did not rule on whether they are false. The campaign compares Zepbound with Wegovy for weight loss and Mounjaro with Ozempic for type 2 diabetes. The case is No. 3:26-cv-09027 in the District of New Jersey.
items.plain: Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly make the competing weight-loss injections. Lilly ran adverts saying its drug works better, and Novo sued, calling the comparison misleading. Novo asked the judge to pull them immediately, before the case is decided. He refused, and the reason is narrow: he did not find the adverts truthful, only that Novo could not show they were costing it enough to justify emergency action. So adverts that may yet be ruled misleading keep running.
items.why: Drugmakers have largely avoided naming rivals in consumer advertising for fear of injunctions, and a ruling that the ads run until a verdict changes that calculation for every branded drug.

items.headline: TSMC is reported to be weighing a 10 to 20 percent rise in advanced packaging prices
items.body: Taiwanese outlets Commercial Times and Economic Daily, relayed by TrendForce on October 27, report that foundries and packaging firms are weighing another round of CoWoS advanced-packaging price increases of 10 to 20 percent, and that TSMC has settled on raising wafer prices 3 to 6 percent from January 2027, steepest on its 2-nanometre and 3-nanometre nodes. Tom's Hardware reported a different 2027 range of 5 to 10 percent. TSMC has confirmed none of it, and every figure rests on unnamed supply-chain sources.
items.plain: A modern AI accelerator is not one chip. It is several pieces of silicon, including stacks of memory, bonded onto a single base and wired together, and TSMC's version of that assembly step is called CoWoS. Those assembly lines, not chipmaking itself, are the narrow part of the pipe, which is why whoever does the assembly can raise prices. Treat the numbers carefully: TSMC has said nothing, and two outlets already give different figures for the same increase.
items.why: Packaging is the real ceiling on how many AI accelerators exist, and because phones and laptops share those lines, a rise there reaches consumer prices before it reaches a data-centre invoice.

items.headline: A judge blocks tree removal at a DC golf course, then orders a top Justice Department official back to explain Trump's own post
items.body: US District Judge Ana Reyes issued a 70-page opinion and preliminary injunction on October 26 barring further removal of trees at East Potomac Golf Links, finding plaintiffs likely to succeed on claims the government split the redevelopment into separate projects to avoid environmental review. At an October 19 hearing, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward had told her, "There is no plan to close the course," and Interior chief of staff Gregory Wischer said he was "not aware" of work set to begin November 15. Reyes wrote that she would credit Trump's own public statements that renovation was beginning immediately over the government's description of the cutting as routine maintenance. Hours after the ruling Trump posted that the course will close November 15 anyway, and Reyes ordered Woodward back into court to say whether his statement still holds. The Justice Department filed a notice of appeal, signed by Woodward.
items.plain: Before cutting trees on federal parkland the government must study the environmental damage first. One way around that is to chop a big project into small pieces, each too minor to require a study. The judge found that likely happened, and she got there unusually: the government's lawyers told her the work was routine with no closure planned, while Trump was publicly saying the opposite, so she believed him over them. He then posted the closure date his lawyers had denied.
items.why: The president's public statements are now being used as evidence against his own Justice Department's representations in court, which costs his lawyers the ability to characterise what he intends.
